vocabmatch.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: Sad because you are far from the place you think of as home
So strong or so much that you cannot deal with it easily
Something good you give up in order to get something else
Time alone that you choose and enjoy
To slowly change your habits so that a new situation feels normal
Strange and slightly frightening, in a very quiet way
To want something so badly that the feeling is almost physical
The confused feeling you get when everything around you works differently

vocabmatch.text: Notice the pair: solitude is alone and GOOD; homesick is alone and BAD. The same empty house, two completely different words.

listenings.text: People always ask me what the hardest part was, and they expect me to say the distance, or the roads, or being far from a hospital. It was none of that. It was the silence. I was used to falling asleep with traffic outside the window, and here there was nothing at all, so for the first month I slept about four hours a night. It was overwhelming in a way I could never explain to anybody who had not done it. Then, somewhere around the fourth month, I stopped noticing. I am not sure when exactly, and that is the strange part, because nobody tells you the day it happens. I only realized it when I went back to the city for a weekend and I could not sleep there either, because the city had become the loud one. That was when I knew I had gotten used to being here. Now I crave it. If I spend three days away I start counting the hours until I am back on that road in the dark.

If you are thinking about moving somewhere much quieter, here is the only honest advice I have. Do not expect to love it in the first month, because you will not. You are not used to the pace yet, and everything that used to take ten minutes now takes an hour. The store closes at six. Nobody delivers anything out here. You have to be a great deal more self-sufficient than you were, and some weeks you simply make do with whatever is in the cupboard. That is the trade-off, and it is a real one, so do not let anybody tell you otherwise. But give it six months. You get used to the driving, you get used to the dark, and then one ordinary morning you walk outside with a cup of coffee and you understand exactly why you came. It grows on you. It just does not grow on you on your schedule.

extra_audio.text: First, Wes says that the power will be off all Thursday morning. Then Ana tells him to charge everything on Wednesday night. Next, Wes admits that he is still not used to planning a whole day around a noticeboard. After that, Ana says that she was exactly the same in her first year. Finally, Wes asks her how long it took before she stopped noticing.
